Ridgeland, MS Girls’ Trip: A 3-Day Itinerary Cocktails, Tea and Vintage

Destinations, USA / By Keryn Means
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 25:39
Instaread

The apple cider Old Fashioned I wanted at Ely’s wasn’t on the menu yet. Spencer, the head bartender who has worked there for nine years, told me the apple cider syrup takes so long to make that he only pours it from about October through February, which makes sense since that is prime cozy weather in Mississippi.

So I ordered the house pineapple-infused vodka martini instead, with a cherry sunk at the bottom of the glass, and settled into one of Ridgeland, Mississippi’s darkest, moodiest dining rooms.

That first sip kicked off a three-day weekend with my friend Tawny. We sipped cocktails at bars and restaurants all over town to test out the Cocktail Passport.

We also squeezed in some vintage shopping (because what’s a trip with Tawny and me without shopping) and afternoon tea at one of the most beautiful tea rooms I’ve ever seen in the States.

Ridgeland sits just north of Jackson along the Natchez Trace Parkway. For a girls’ getaway, it offers a free cocktail and culinary passport, an open-air shopping center with restaurants and bars (make sure you check out the free Ridgeland Culinary Passport too!), a Southern tea room, and a stretch of Highway 51 lined with thrift and antique stores.

If you’re building a Mississippi trip, it pairs well with my Tupelo girls’ trip itinerary, as well as my Franklin, TN and Leiper’s Fork, TN, itineraries, all along the Natchez Trace Parkway.

Come hungry, because you are about to eat and drink a lot.

This trip was part of a project with Explore Ridgeland. As always, my opinions are my own. When they aren’t, you will be the first to know.

Ridgeland Girls’ Trip Quick Facts

  • Where: Ridgeland, Mississippi, just north of Jackson
  • Fly into: Jackson-Medgar Wiley Evers International Airport (JAN), about 20 minutes south of Ridgeland by car.
  • Where to stay: AC Hotel by Marriott Jackson Ridgeland, 221 Township Ave., with free parking but no pool.
  • Getting around: Drive or take a rideshare. Many stops are clustered inside Renaissance at Colony Park, which is easy to walk around.
  • Plan: Sign up for the free Explore Ridgeland Cocktail Passport and Culinary Passport before your first stop.
  • Weekday-only stop: The Ridgeland Visitors Center, where you pick up passport prizes, is closed on weekends, but you can access the mural outside anytime.

Is Ridgeland, MS Good for a Girls’ Trip?

Yes, especially if your group plans weekends around food and drinks. Most of what we did sat within a short drive of the hotel, and much of it was inside Renaissance at Colony Park, where you can park once and walk between shopping, cocktails and dinner.

It also has a few quiet stops to slow things down, like a paved trail through the woods and a city wildflower field. For more small-city girls’ weekends, see my Fargo and Bowling Green itineraries.

How the Ridgeland Cocktail and Culinary Passports Work

The Explore Ridgeland Cocktail Passport and Culinary Passport are free, mobile-only digital passes. You sign up on the Explore Ridgeland Experiences page, and the pass arrives by text and email.

There’s no app to download. You save the link to your home screen, then check in at each participating restaurant or bar using your phone’s GPS (location services).

Cost: Nothing to join. You pay only for what you order at each stop.

How points work: Each check-in earns 100 points. At 300 points, you unlock a prize; at 600 points, you unlock another prize tier, and you can pick up prizes during office hours at the Ridgeland Visitors Center.

The two trails: The Cocktail Passport features a drink at each stop, and the Culinary Passport highlights a special menu item. Many businesses are on both passports, but you check in on each pass separately to earn points at both.

A few tips for using it:

  • Turn on location services, including Precise Location on an iPhone, before you walk in. If a check-in doesn’t register, step closer to the entrance or go outside, since GPS can be wonky sometimes.
  • You can still check in if you order something that isn’t the featured item.
  • After you check in, the same business resets in four hours, so a second visit later in the weekend counts again.
  • You must be 21 or older to sign up for and use the Cocktail Passport.

Sign up for both passes on the drive from the airport, and plan one weekday stop at the Visitors Center if you want to claim a prize in person. It’s open Monday through Friday, 9 a.m. to 5 p.m.

The Passport Stops We Hit

You don’t have to order the featured drink to check in, but it helps to know what each stop is known for. Keep in mind that the passport listings do change, so don’t be surprised if one or more aren’t on the menu during your visit. You can always ask them to make one for you though, as most of these cocktails use ingredients usually found behind the bar. 

Arrival Night (Thursday)

Arriving in Jackson, MS, feels like landing in most smaller cities. It’s easy to navigate; the car rental pickup is right there, and you can be on your way to your first stop in under an hour. A far cry from my LAX experience at home.

I grabbed my rental car while I waited for Tawny’s flight to get in, then picked her up at the curb as she exited.

We drove the 20 minutes up to Ridgeland, dropped our bags, freshened up our makeup and headed out to dinner.

Dinner at Ely’s

Ely’s Restaurant & Bar is a dark, low-lit spot locals love for date night, but it’s just as good for a girls’ night over great food and drinks. The owner, Richard, keeps the food and drinks consistent; the staff is super friendly, and the menu shows Lebanese influences, which is pretty unexpected in Mississippi.

We kicked off our meal with fried artichokes, battered and fried like fried pickles, so if you like those, you’ll love these. I had the redfish, which comes with a tabbouleh salad starter, while Tawny stuck with a steak.

Two drinks you will want to order:

  • The cucumber martini, made with a cucumber-lime syrup, is strong and cool, like a spa in a glass but much boozier.
  • The pineapple-infused vodka martini leans hard into pineapple and packs a deceptively strong punch. You can also order it on the rocks.

The apple cider Old Fashioned is Ely’s featured Cocktail Passport drink, but it’s only offered seasonally. Spencer, the head bartender, makes the syrup from scratch by reducing apple cider with nutmeg, cinnamon sticks and other spices.

He told me it’s one of the drinks he’s proudest of and took a long time to perfect. Look for it from about October through February.

My Pumpkin Old Fashioned is a good fall stand-in at home if you aren’t headed to Ely’s this season.

I’d make a reservation at Ely’s just in case, especially on a weekend.

Day 1 (Friday): Acai Bowls, Afternoon Tea and the Renaissance Bars

Breakfast at Whirl Smoothie Bar & Coffee House

I need (and I do mean NEED, or the hangry monster pops out of me) to start my day with fresh produce, so Whirl Smoothie Bar & Coffee House was our first stop. Tawny and I loved it so much we went two mornings in a row.

The acai bowl is a thick smoothie base topped with berries, banana and granola. It comes with peanut butter, but I prefer mine without, since it just tastes like a PB&J sandwich.

The large Maple Leaf Shaken Espresso gave me all the protein I needed to tackle the morning, as it was mostly milk. Still counts!

Coffee purists will be happy with the regular espresso drinks and drip coffee. The specialty drinks are inventive, and you can ask them to adjust the sweetness level.

The Ridgeland Bikeshare rack is just down the driveway from Whirl, near an entrance to the Chisha Foka Multi-Use Trail, a paved path that runs about 10 miles through historic Choctaw homelands. It was way too hot and steamy for us to tackle the trail during our visit, but if you are looking for an easy workout, I’d rent bikes before or after breakfast.

Rentals run through the Koloni app, and each bike includes a helmet in its basket, which will make this mom VERY happy if I bring my kids back next time. Even though the idea of doing anything outside would make me melt, it was nice to know the bikes are available from sunrise to sunset.

Grab a Photo at the Welcome to Ridgeland Mural

We stopped for our photo at the “Welcome to Ridgeland” mural, along a wall just outside the Ridgeland Visitors Center at the Renaissance. It’s a great spot for that postcard photo everyone is showing off right now, plus you can pop in to grab more ideas and information from the staff inside.

The Visitors Center opens at 9 a.m. and is only open on weekdays, so I’d swing by after breakfast on Friday. The mural is there all the time, so you don’t have to worry about closing times if you are only visiting on the weekend.

Ridgeland Wildflower Field

The Ridgeland Wildflower Field is another great spot to wander through nature. It’s a short drive from almost anywhere in Ridgeland, and it sits in a huge field right off the highway overpass.

We took a morning stroll through the gardens and saw loads of bees and butterflies. Zinnias were the main flower in bloom at the time, but like all flowers, what you see depends on the season.

Afternoon Tea at CW Organics Apothicaire & Tea Room

If I’m on a girls’ trip, I never say no to afternoon tea. My boys loathe it now because I dragged them to so many when they were little. Tawny, like me, loves a funky space with good food and drinks, so we headed to CW Organics Apothicaire & Tea Room to meet owner Caroline Warner and learn why this shop is so unique.

Walking into CW Organics, we felt like we were magically transported to an old shop in Paris or someone’s greenhouse. I loved everything about the space and wanted to take it home immediately.

Apparently, I’ll have to kidnap her husband, Jack, as he built the hutch, bar, shelves and tables by hand. It was more than the furniture, though; Caroline’s attention to detail really drew us in.

No two pieces of china on your table match, because Ridgeland residents donated most of the dishware after Caroline asked on social media for old china sets and dishes when she was converting her retail shop into a cafe/retail space.

The shelves are lined with glass jars of tea, most of which Caroline custom-blends herself. And there were dried flowers EVERYWHERE. When I asked how her flowers kept their color even when dried, she told me the secret that changed the way I dry plants: hang them upside down while they are still fresh, not once they are sad and wilted.

As for the food, Caroline wanted to set up a Southern tea room rather than an English one. That means her tiered tray carries pimento cheese, chicken salad and scratch biscuits alongside the scones.

Pair that with a Papaya & Butterfly Pea Flower Iced Herbal Tea that looks prettier than most cocktails, and you have the perfect lunchtime or afternoon tea. The iced teas are a great non-alcoholic option, and Caroline also blends remedy teas for things like sinus trouble, sleep and immunity.

CW Organics is on the Culinary Passport. A few more details that will help with planning:

  • You can split a tray for one between friends or order à la carte.
  • If you can’t finish your pot, she’ll send you off with a to-go cup.
  • There’s no dress code. Caroline wants you to feel comfortable and welcome just as you are.

If you’re new to herbal tea, Caroline steers first-timers toward White Strawberry, her most popular blend, or a Lavender and Lemon tea. You can also tell her how you’re feeling, and she’ll blend something to match.

I wrote a full profile of Caroline Warner and how she built the shop, from pulling weeds on her grandparents’ Delta farm to opening the tea room. Check it out on ExploreRidgeland.com.

Afternoon Cocktails at Anjou

After our tea and herbal education, we headed back to the AC Hotel to freshen up, then walked next door to Anjou, a French-inspired restaurant with a spot on both passports. Its featured drink, the Anjou cocktail, mixes vodka, Chambord, and pineapple, and it’s sweet and fruit-forward thanks to the Chambord.

I tend to shy away from super-sweet drinks these days, so the Whiskey Smash (bourbon, fresh mint, lemon juice and a splash of sweet and sour) was the perfect Southern alternative for me. It isn’t too boozy, which was good since we had cocktails to check off the passport.

If you like that style, my Prickly Pear Bourbon Smash is an easy one to make at home.

Cocktails and Dinner at Koestler Prime

Koestler Prime is a moody bar and restaurant inside the Renaissance, with some of the area’s most knowledgeable bartenders and a back bar stocked with top-shelf bottles. As a gin drinker, I went straight for the gin drinks.

The Prime 75 is a more herbal take on a French 75, with Roku gin, St-Germain, lemon, honey, ginger and chamomile, topped with bubbles. If you like that one, try my Orange Blossom Earl Grey French 75 at home.

The Sage and Spirit is still Koestler’s featured drink on the Cocktail Passport, but it hasn’t been on the menu for about two years. You can still check in without it, and The Last Word is a good replacement. The Last Word is a classic cocktail invented around 1915. Made with equal parts gin, green Chartreuse, maraschino liqueur and fresh lime juice, this drink doesn’t get sweet and stays in that nice herbaceous zone.

If you are a craft cocktail lover, you know Green Chartreuse is scarce and in high demand these days, so it’s hard to get your hands on even one bottle. Happily, my bartender passed along a tip for home cocktail makers like me: Génépy is a good stand-in for Green Chartreuse.

I also left with the suggestion to try Another Hendrix gin (yes, that’s the name) in a Ramos Gin Fizz.

Obviously, you can’t drink on an empty stomach, so we ordered steak for Tawny (she gobbled it up, so I assume it was good) and fish for me (give me salmon in a lemon-dill sauce any day, and I’ll be happy). We kept chatting with the bartenders before calling it a night, with another stop checked off the Cocktail Passport.

As with Ely’s, I’d make a reservation just in case, especially on a weekend.

Day 2 (Saturday): Shopping, a Frozen Flight and Bourbon at TASTE

Shopping at Renaissance at Colony Park

After Friday’s eating fest, we knew we had to do a little shopping on Saturday to burn off a few calories. Don’t worry, we still had breakfast at Whirl first (again, although the AC Hotel has a nice breakfast buffet too).

We started our shopping journey at Renaissance at Colony Park, an open-air shopping center with shops and restaurants. It’s close to the AC Hotel, so it’s easy to pop back if you decide you want that dress from the Anthropologie sales rack after all (yes, it happened).

You’ll find the usual shops like Sephora, Columbia Sportswear, Pandora, Anthropologie (the sales rack was epic during our visit), the Apple Store, and Aerie. There is even a Barnes & Noble there still!

If you linger after dark (between about 6 p.m. and 9 p.m.), the Renaissance fountain lights up like the Bellagio in Vegas, which is both fun for little ones and a cool stop for us gals hopping between restaurants.

Lunch and a Frozen Flight at Aplos

Aplos, a Mediterranean spot inside the Renaissance, sells a frozen cocktail flight with four flavors: Frosé, Med Breeze, Peach Please, and Porch Swing, perfect if you’re not sure which one you’ll like.

Personally, I liked the Frosé and Peach Please best. The Med Breeze and Porch Swing were both too tart for me.

If you’re ordering one full-size drink instead, Tawny said the Watermelon Mule was excellent. I tried one of the non-alcoholic options: the Refresher mocktail (cucumber, lavender, lemon, lime and soda) was tasty and a chill way to cool off mid-afternoon.

Before we even arrived, our friend Tammilee told us to get the whipped feta at Aplos, and as always, she was not wrong (she even has a recipe for it on her site). I mean, I’m down for any feta, but make it smooth enough to dip in, and suddenly I’m eating a whole lot more bread than I normally do.

I don’t regret a bite. Tawny and I split the chicken shawarma wrap, which was just as good.

Aplos isn’t your typical sit-down restaurant. You order at a counter, get a number and find yourself a seat. If you sit at the bar, you can order straight from the bartender, which is what we did.

Antique and Vintage Shopping off Highway 51

If you didn’t know already, Tawny and I are huge fans of thrifting and vintage shopping. I love a good hunt, and we always come back with treasures we’re not quite sure we will get home.

Just a short drive from the Renaissance, you’ll find a cluster of antique and secondhand stores along U.S. Highway 51. These three are my favorites, and they’re all within five minutes of each other:

  • Antique Aly, 294 Commerce Park Drive
  • Antique Mall of the South, 367 U.S. 51
  • Mid-Century & More Vintage, 295 U.S. 51

If you have more time, check out the local thrift store scene, including:

  • Goodwill Ridgeland Supercenter (379 U.S. 51)
  • Palladian Consign & Design (637 U.S. 51)
  • St. Andrew’s Thrift Store (869 S. Pear Orchard Road)

At Mid-Century & More Vintage, I finally found a Blendo pitcher and tumbler set I’ve been looking for forever, at an affordable price. I also picked up some new-to-me vintage cocktail glasses at the other shops we stopped in.

Sadly, one of the tumblers didn’t make it home in my suitcase, but the set still works just fine for me.

Bourbon and the Whiskey Is Bananas at TASTE Italian Kitchen

After we shopped til we dropped (I couldn’t walk through vast warehouses of awesome anymore, and my credit card was yelling at me), we headed back to the Renaissance for a little “Bubble Hour” at TASTE Italian Kitchen.

Instead of Happy Hour, this restaurant and bar likes to kick off the evening with an Aperol Spritz on the outdoor patio from 4 to 6 p.m. daily. Tawny was thrilled.

Lucky for me, the anti-Aperol gal, the bar carries more than 300 bourbons, scotches, whiskeys and ryes, plus more than 200 wines. Connor Morris, the restaurant and bar manager, made us the Whiskey Is Bananas (rye, banana and chicory pecan bitters), the bar’s featured Cocktail Passport drink.

The idea was to get something close to banana bread, and I think they did pretty darn well.

The one thing I didn’t get to try was the Ginepro & Tonico. Morris makes it with Empress 1908 gin, quinine powder and lime, the way a gin and tonic was made before bottled tonic water.

He also stocks Mississippi spirits, including Cathead Distillery’s Old Soul State Collection and Wonderbird gin from Taylor, Mississippi (check out or order their magnolia gin. You’re welcome).

I wrote a full profile of Morris and the TASTE bar program on ExploreRidgeland.com if you want to learn more.

Dinner at Local 463

At this point, we weren’t sure whether we needed dinner or a nap, but Local 463 sits inside the Renaissance, so how could we pass up this spot on our last night? The Pomegranate Fizz, which runs sweet, is featured on the Ridgeland Cocktail Passport.

Tawny loved it, and she goes sweeter with her cocktails, but I preferred the 463, a strawberry-and-basil cocktail. The strawberry and basil work well together, though the basil comes through strongest. I’d back off the basil a little if I make it at home.

The watermelon feta salad is huge and fresh, making it easy to share, while the flounder and steak are still something Tawny and I talk about.

Day 3 (Sunday): Brunch at Amerigo and the Natchez Trace Parkway

Take a Stroll along the Natchez Trace Parkway

While it was a little out of the way from the main highlights of my weekend trip (and by little, I mean a 5-10 minute detour), the Natchez Trace Parkway was the perfect escape from the highways surrounding Ridgeland. For those from the Mid-Atlantic, it felt much like the Colonial Parkway.

We were short on time, so we just drove to the Reservoir Overlook for gorgeous water views and one last group photo. If you have more time for a hike, head farther up the Chisha Foka Multi-Use Trail, or check out Old Trace Park for easy walks along the Parkway.

Sunday Brunch at Amerigo

We wrapped up the weekend with Sunday brunch at Amerigo, our last Cocktail and Culinary Passport stop before we headed to the airport.

I had their specialty French toast with a side of eggs and bacon, while Tawny enjoyed a Caesar salad and fettuccine Alfredo (she’s weird and likes lunch for her brunch).

Naturally, we ordered the Cocktail Passport drink, the Ginger Cat, which tastes tropical thanks to the pineapple juice in the mix. We also got the Whisky Fizz, which was slightly sweet with plenty of fizz, making it the perfect brunch cocktail, at least for me.

Where to Stay in Ridgeland: AC Hotel by Marriott Jackson Ridgeland

I stayed at the AC Hotel by Marriott Jackson Ridgeland at 221 Township Ave. It’s close to Renaissance at Colony Park, so most of the shops, restaurants and bars I was visiting were only a few minutes away.

Parking is free, the staff is kind to everyone who walks in, and the rooms are super comfy with great air conditioning. There is no pool, though, so if that’s important, check out another Ridgeland, MS hotel.

The AC Lounge is also on the Cocktail Passport, making this an easy first check-in when I arrived. Its featured drink, the Suckle and Stinger, is made with Mississippi’s Cathead Honeysuckle Vodka, lemon, local honey and bitters, making it a sweet welcome (although I’d ask them to skip the bitters next time).

Find the best rates at the AC Hotel on Expedia.

How to Get to Ridgeland, MS

The closest airport to Ridgeland is Jackson-Medgar Wiley Evers International Airport (JAN), about 20 minutes south of Ridgeland. I flew in from Los Angeles, and it’s a long trek, so I arrived Thursday so I’d have two full days to explore.

Set fare alerts with Going a few months out and book when a deal to JAN shows up.

You will definitely want a car. While shops and restaurants inside the Renaissance are walkable, favorite spots like Whirl, CW Organics, Ely’s, Amerigo, and the antique stores off Highway 51 require a car, as does getting to and from the airport.

Discover Cars lets you compare rental companies at JAN side by side. Just remember: if you or anyone in your group is drinking, use a designated driver or rideshare for the cocktail stops so you all make it back to the hotel safely.

To map out who’s driving, who’s booking dinner and which passport stops you’ll hit, use my free weekend trip planner.

How Many Days Do You Need in Ridgeland?

For a quick getaway, three days is all you probably need. Friday allows you to squeeze in any weekday-only stops, including the Visitors Center and a slower afternoon at CW Organics. Saturday is always a great day for shopping and the Renaissance bars and restaurants, while Sunday morning leaves time for brunch before the airport.

For your next quick girls’ trip, check out my itineraries for St. Augustine, Quebec City and Calgary.

Planning a Fall Trip to Ridgeland

If you go between October and February, start your weekend at Ely’s. That’s when Spencer’s apple cider syrup is back on the stove, and the drink he’s proudest of is back on the menu.
